narrative: Your application was unfortunately rejected because the model estimated a 51% probability that you would not pass the bar exam on your first attempt. This prediction means the model views your current academic profile as being just on the edge of a passing grade, but slightly favoring a negative outcome. While your undergraduate GPA of 3.70 is impressively higher than the 3.24 average of students who typically pass, other academic indicators suggest a higher risk of struggle during the bar. Specifically, your law school performance placed you in the bottom 30% during your first year and the bottom 10% by your third year. This ranking contrasts sharply with the average passing student, who typically ranks in the top 40% of their class by the end of their studies. To understand how this decision could be reversed, we analyzed three "what if" scenarios that identify the smallest changes needed to predict a successful exam outcome. These scenarios represent alternative paths where your application would have been approved despite your current class rankings. In every single one of these scenarios, the model identified your LSAT score as the most critical factor to address. While your current score is 34, the analysis shows that increasing this score by just two points to a 36 would be enough to flip the prediction to a passing grade. Interestingly, the model did not require you to change your part-time status or account for your lower-middle family income level to reach this positive result. This suggests that despite the challenges of balancing law school with other responsibilities, a slightly stronger foundation in the skills measured by the LSAT is the primary bridge to success. By focusing your efforts on retaking the exam and achieving that 36, you would align your profile much more closely with the 37.27 average seen in successful candidates. This specific, two-point improvement was the only change required across 100% of the successful alternative scenarios generated. Other factors, such as your undergraduate performance and your status as a part-time student, remained constant in these successful paths. This indicates that your current undergraduate foundation is already strong enough to support a passing result if the LSAT score is improved. Because your predicted failure was only at 51%, you are very close to the threshold, and this small adjustment makes all the difference. Focusing on this one area provides a clear, singular roadmap for a successful re-application in the future.
